lines.text: Where does bile salt reuptake principally occur?
The answer is in the ileum.
The happy ileum opens its arms. This is where bile salts are taken back up.
Between ninety and ninety-five per cent of bile salts are absorbed from the small intestine, mostly from the terminal ileum.
(laugh) They ride their wagon along the golden road of the enterohepatic circulation.
Back at the liver, they are excreted again into bile.
The whole pool recycles twice per meal, about six to eight times a day.
Remember: bile salt reuptake happens in the ileum, mainly the terminal ileum.
A forty-year-old is brought into A and E with a head injury. What are the cardiovascular effects of raised intracranial pressure?
The answer is: blood pressure up, heart rate down, and cerebral perfusion pressure down.
His skull is a steaming pressure cooker. The intracranial pressure is rising.
The adult brain sits in a rigid box, so the volume inside must stay constant.
He holds the formula. Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
So as the intracranial pressure rises, perfusion pressure and cerebral blood flow fall.
The gauge shows blood pressure going up.
(sigh) And the tired heart rides a snail. The heart rate goes down.
Remember: raised intracranial pressure means blood pressure up, heart rate down, and perfusion pressure down.
